answers.text: Same as before, every supplier email is a little different, so I would tell the AI: give me exactly three lines, always in this order — delivery date, then item and quantity, then any change from the original order. That way the summary reads the same shape every time, whichever email goes in.

For the expense claims, I would say: list every claim as one row with date, amount, category, submitter, in that order, and then add up the amount column at the bottom so the total is always calculated the same way, not typed in by hand.

Reading it again, the problem is the dates, not the price — the call was on the 14th, but the text says the new date is the 19th and also calls that 'three days out from today', and those two do not match up, since the 19th is five days after the 14th. The €4,850 total is correct as 100 times 48.50, so it is not that.
62 up from 54 is about right for 15%. But 3 late out of 62 works out closer to 95%, not the 97% stated, so that is the one I would flag.

I would sign off Output 2 since it gives the actual sales and returns numbers behind the 4.1%, not just the final figure. Output 1 might well be right, but there is nothing in it to check it against, so you would have to just trust it.

I would send Reply 2 straight away — the order reference and credit reference mean someone can look them up. Reply 1 is not necessarily wrong, but until you have references for the 'our error' claim and the credit, you cannot check it, so it needs someone to confirm those first before it goes out too.

1. No — that is the customer's own address, personal information. 2. Yes — it is just an aggregate total, no one is identifiable in it. 3. No — pricing for next quarter has not been released yet, so it should not go outside the team. 4. Yes — it is already published on our website, so there is nothing new being exposed. 5. No — a colleague's personal mobile number is not mine to hand over.

The pricing and discount figures I would treat carefully, and the confidentiality clause too, since it names both companies — those I would hold back until the tool is cleared. For the rest I would rather leave it all out than guess which bits are fine.
I would build in a step where I check the total deliveries figure against the depot log before the report goes out on Friday, not after it has already gone up.

Step 1 already carries risk, because if the AI misreads the quantity there, everything downstream is built on that wrong number. But the step that most needs a gate is step 4 — once the confirmation email goes out automatically, you cannot pull it back, so that is where a check matters most. The gate should hold back and route to a person anything where stock in step 2 is close to the limit, or where step 1 could not read the order cleanly, rather than letting it go straight out. If the gate blocks something, it should land with whoever is on order-processing that day, not just sit there.
